modules.title: Reading Hair and Scalp Before Every Service
modules.overview: Every safe service starts before the first part is made. In this module you learn a five-minute hands-on hair assessment, a scalp check that tells you when to serve, postpone or refer, and a written consultation that matches the style to the hair in front of you.

lessons.title: The hands-on hair assessment: density, strand width, porosity and elasticity
objectives: Test a client's hair density at the crown, hairline and nape
Judge strand width by comparing a shed hair with sewing thread
Observe porosity and elasticity during the wash
Turn your four findings into a style, size and tension decision

blocks.text: A client sits down and says, "I want small knotless braids, waist length." A beginner starts parting. A professional first spends about five minutes looking at the hair, because the same style can be safe on one head and harmful on another. This lesson gives you four simple checks that need nothing more than your hands, a tail comb, a spray bottle of clean water, a strand of sewing thread and good light.

blocks.name: left-pointing-magnifying-glass
blocks.caption: Look closely before you agree to any style: four quick checks guide every decision in this course.

blocks.text: Check 1: density (how much hair there is)

Density means how many strands grow on each part of the scalp. It is not the same as how thick each strand is. To test it, make a straight part at the crown on dry hair and look at how much scalp you can see. If the scalp is hard to see, density is high. If you see a clear line of scalp, it is medium. If the scalp shows easily even before you part, density is low. Repeat at the front hairline, the temples and the nape, because density is rarely the same everywhere. The temples and edges are often the thinnest part of the head, and they are also the part that suffers most from tight styling.
Check 2: strand width (fine, medium or coarse)

Pick up one shed strand from her comb or shoulders. Hold it next to a piece of ordinary sewing thread. If the hair looks thinner than the thread and you can hardly feel it when you roll it between finger and thumb, it is fine. If it is about the same, it is medium. If it feels wiry and thicker than the thread, it is coarse. Fine strands break more easily under tension and heat, so a client with fine hair needs gentler handling and less added weight, even if she has plenty of hair.
Check 3: porosity (how hair takes in and loses water)

Porosity describes how easily water gets into the strand and how quickly it leaves again. It depends on the cuticle, the outer layer of overlapping scales. You observe it during the wash rather than guessing. Spray a small clean section with water. If the water sits in droplets on top and the hair takes a long time to get wet and a long time to dry, porosity is low. If the hair soaks up water at once, dries quickly and feels rough or frizzes, porosity is high. Ends that have been coloured, relaxed or heated often behave differently from the roots, so test both.
Check 4: elasticity (how hair stretches and returns)

items: Take one wet strand from the back of the head, where it will not be missed.
Hold it firmly near the root with one hand so you do not pull the scalp.
With the other hand, stretch the strand slowly and gently, then release.

Healthy hair stretches a little and springs back. Hair that snaps almost at once is dry and brittle. Hair that stretches a long way, feels gummy and stays stretched is weak and needs very gentle handling.
Write the result on her card. Never repeat the test on the same strand.

blocks.title: Five-minute hair assessment
items: Density at four places
Strand width against thread
Porosity during the wash
Elasticity of one strand
Record it on her card
blocks.caption: Do all four checks and write them down before you quote a style or a price.

blocks.title: Worked example: from findings to a safer style
blocks.context: For example, Amaka runs a home salon in Enugu. Her client Funmi asks for small waist-length knotless braids for a wedding.
steps: Crown parting: scalp is visible along the part, so density is medium. At both temples the scalp shows easily, so the edges are low density.
Strand width: Funmi's shed strand looks thinner than the sewing thread, so her hair is fine.
During the wash, water sits on top of the hair for a while and the hair takes a long time to dry: low porosity.
Elasticity: the strand stretches a little and springs back: healthy.

Decision: fine hair with thin temples should not carry many small, heavy, waist-length braids. Amaka recommends medium knotless braids at mid-back length, with the temple hair left free or braided with no added hair, and she allows extra drying time because low-porosity hair dries slowly.
blocks.result: Funmi still gets knotless braids for the wedding, but in a size and length her hair can carry. Amaka writes all four findings on the record card so she can compare next time.

blocks.title: Use good light
blocks.text: Do the checks by a window in daylight or with a phone torch. Dim light hides thin patches at the temples and makes density look higher than it is.

Hair changes. A client who wore heavy braids for months, had a baby, changed diet or started colouring can have very different hair from her last visit. Repeat the assessment at every service, even for regular clients, and compare it with what you wrote last time. When the edges look thinner than before, say so kindly and plan a lighter style. That honest note is one of the most valuable things a stylist can give a client.

takeaways: Density is how many strands there are; strand width is how thick each one is. Check both.
Test density in four places: crown, hairline, temples and nape.
Observe porosity and elasticity during the wash, not by guessing.
Fine hair and thin edges mean bigger sections, less added hair and gentler tension.
Repeat the assessment at every visit and compare with your notes.

activity.title: Assess three heads
steps: Ask three people (family or friends) if you may assess their hair.
Do all four checks in good light on each person.
Record density at four places, strand width, porosity and elasticity on a simple card.
For each person, write one style size you would recommend and one you would avoid, with the reason.
Compare the three cards and note which check surprised you most.
activity.evidence: Three completed assessment cards with your recommendation and reason on each

lessons.title: Scalp checks: when to serve, postpone or refer
objectives: Carry out a systematic scalp check before washing or combing
Recognise signs that mean you should postpone a service and refer the client
Explain a problem privately and kindly without diagnosing
Clean your tools correctly after finding lice or a suspected infection

blocks.text: Your hands touch more scalps in a month than many health workers do. That makes you an important early warning. It does not make you a doctor. Your job is to notice, to protect the client and your next clients, and to point her to the right help. You never diagnose and you never recommend or apply medicine. This lesson shows you how to look, what to look for, and what to do with what you find.

blocks.name: medical-care
blocks.alt: A health worker caring for a patient
blocks.caption: Some scalp signs belong with a health worker, not in the salon chair.

blocks.text: How to do the scalp check

items: Wash your hands and seat the client in good light, before you wet or comb the hair.
Ask: "Is any part of your scalp sore, itchy or tender? Have you had any treatment, relaxer or colour in the last two weeks?"
Using the tail of a clean comb, make parts about two finger-widths apart from the front hairline back to the nape.
Look along every part, and specially at the hairline, temples, crown, behind the ears and the nape.
If you see broken skin, sores or pus, put on disposable gloves before you touch the area again.
Write what you saw on the client card, even when everything is healthy.

blocks.text: What you might see and what to do

head: What you see
What it may mean
What you do
rows: Light white flakes, no redness, no pain
Serve. Cleanse gently, note it on the card. If it persists, suggest she asks a pharmacist or health worker.
Live insects, or tiny eggs (nits) glued to strands close to the scalp
Do not serve today. Tell her privately. Suggest she seeks advice from a health worker or pharmacist. Clean your tools as described below.
Round or patchy scaly areas with broken hairs or hair loss, sometimes itchy
Possible ringworm of the scalp (a fungal infection)
Do not serve. Refer to a clinic or health worker. It can spread on shared combs and towels.
Bumps, spots or pus around old braid bases, or soreness
Irritation or infection, often linked to tension
Do not re-braid tightly. Refer if there is pus, spreading redness or fever.
Thinning or bare areas at the temples or hairline
Possible tension-related hair loss or another hair loss condition
No tension on that area. Suggest a health worker or dermatologist assessment.
Cuts, scratches, burns or raw skin
No chemicals on that area. Avoid braiding over it. Refer if it looks infected.

blocks.title: Serve, postpone or refer
items: Look and ask first
Record what you see
Contagious sign? Postpone, refer
Sore or broken skin? Avoid, refer
Healthy? Start the service
blocks.caption: Make the decision before the wash, so a problem never spreads to your tools, towels or the next client.

blocks.title: Facts about head lice
blocks.text: According to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), head lice cannot hop or fly. They spread mainly through direct contact with the hair of a person who has lice, and also through shared combs, brushes, towels, hats and scarves. Adult lice usually die within two days off the head.
Saying it kindly and privately

Clients feel embarrassed about lice or ringworm, and mothers worry they will be blamed. Never announce what you found in front of other clients. Step aside and use calm words: "I noticed some patches on her scalp that I am not trained to judge. I don't want to braid over them and make them worse. Please let a health worker look at it first, and I will keep your booking for when she is cleared." Avoid naming a condition as a fact. Say what you saw, not what you think it is.
Cleaning tools after a problem scalp

Put every comb, clip and towel you touched into a separate bag. For lice, the CDC advises soaking combs and brushes in hot water of at least about 54°C (130°F) for 5 to 10 minutes, and washing towels and capes on a hot cycle. For a suspected fungal infection, wash tools with soap and water, then disinfect them as you will learn in Module 4. Wash your hands for a full 40 to 60 seconds afterwards.

blocks.title: Worked example: two sisters, one problem
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kaduna has a booking to cornrow two sisters aged 7 and 9. Their mother paid a deposit of about ₦2,000 by transfer.
steps: During the scalp check, Halima sees two round scaly patches with broken hairs on the younger girl's crown.
She stops, puts that comb and towel in a bag, and checks the older sister carefully with a fresh comb. Her scalp looks healthy.
She speaks to the mother privately, describes what she saw, and suggests the clinic before the younger girl's hair is done.
She braids the older sister with fresh tools and keeps the ₦2,000 deposit as credit for the younger girl's appointment.
After the session she washes and disinfects every tool, and writes the date and what she saw on both girls' cards.
blocks.result: One child is served safely, the other is referred without embarrassment, no tools carry the problem to other clients, and the family's money is kept as credit, so the mother trusts Halima and comes back.

blocks.title: Stay within your role
blocks.text: Never recommend a medicine, give a dose, or apply any treatment to a scalp problem. Never put relaxer, colour or any chemical on broken or sore skin. Your role is to stop, protect and refer.

takeaways: Check the scalp in good light before washing or combing.
Postpone and refer for signs of lice, possible ringworm, pus, sores or bald patches.
Describe what you saw privately; do not diagnose.
Bag and clean every tool that touched a problem scalp before using it again.
Write every finding on the client card, including healthy ones.

activity.title: Build your scalp check card
steps: Draw a simple head outline on a card with six zones: hairline, temples, crown, behind ears, nape, and other.
Do a scalp check on two willing family members and mark anything you see in each zone.
Write the serve, postpone or refer decision for each person.
Write and practise aloud your own private script for telling a client about a problem.
List where in your area a client could be referred: the nearest clinic, primary health centre or pharmacy.
activity.evidence: Two filled scalp check cards, your written script and your referral list

lessons.title: The consultation and client record card
objectives: Run a structured consultation that ends in a clear written agreement
Match the requested style to the hair assessment and the client's routine
Estimate service time and quote it before you start
Record consent for photos and for children's services

blocks.text: Most salon arguments start with a gap between what the client imagined and what the stylist delivered: the braids were bigger, it took longer, the price grew, the edges were pulled. A short, structured consultation closes that gap. It also protects her hair, because you agree on a style her hair can carry. Ten minutes of questions and writing saves hours of disagreement.

blocks.name: complete-form
blocks.alt: A person filling in a form
blocks.caption: A simple written card turns a chat into a clear agreement.

blocks.text: The record card

Use a notebook page, a printed card or a note on your phone for each client. Keep it private: it holds personal information, so do not share it or post it in groups. Fill in these fields at every visit.

head: Field
What to write
rows: First name and WhatsApp number she agrees to share
Density in four places, strand width, porosity, elasticity
Healthy, or what you saw and the decision
Last style and when it was removed, any relaxer or colour and the date
Any itching, rash or soreness from products or extensions in the past
Style name, size, length, colour, who supplies the hair
Estimated hours and the agreed total, deposit paid
Photos allowed: yes or no. For a child: parent's name and agreement

blocks.text: Questions that reveal what she really needs

items: **"What is the occasion and when is it?"** A wedding in ten days needs a different plan from a back-to-school style.
**"How long do you want to keep it in?"** This tells you how much growth and wear the style must survive.
**"How do you sleep and exercise?"** A client who trains daily needs a style that dries quickly and can be tied up.
**"Can you show me a picture?"** Then point to the size and length and confirm them in words.
**"Has any style ever been painful or left bumps?"** Her answer tells you how careful to be with tension.

blocks.title: Request versus reality
items: What she asks for
What you check
blocks.caption: A good consultation brings the two sides together before you agree on anything.

blocks.text: Estimating time before you quote

Clients want to know how long they will sit. Use your own timed average per braid or row, not a guess. Count how many sections the style needs, multiply by your minutes per section, then add the wash, drying and finishing. You will build your personal timing log in Module 4. Until then, time yourself on practice heads and use those numbers.

blocks.title: Worked example: a consultation that changes the plan
blocks.context: For example, Chioma runs a salon corner in Onitsha. A client wants small knotless braids, waist length, for a wedding in ten days.
steps: Assessment shows medium density at the crown and thin temples. Chioma explains that waist-length small braids would hang heavily on thin edges.
They agree on medium knotless braids, mid-back length, with the temple hair braided without added hair.
Chioma counts the plan: 8 rows with an average of 10 braids per row gives 8 x 10 = 80 braids.
Her timed average for medium knotless is 6 minutes per braid: 80 x 6 = 480 minutes, which is 8 hours of braiding.

She adds 30 minutes for washing and 60 minutes for drying and stretching: 480 + 30 + 60 = 570 minutes, which is 9 hours 30 minutes in total. She writes this on the card with the agreed price and takes a deposit.
blocks.result: The client knows the style, size, length, time and price in advance. She chooses to come two days before the wedding, starting at 8 a.m., and nothing about the day is a surprise.

blocks.text: When she insists on a style her hair cannot carry

Sometimes a client hears your advice and still wants the tiny, heavy, very long braids. Explain once, calmly, what you saw: "Your temples are thinner than the rest of your hair, and this length adds a lot of weight there." Offer two safer versions of the look she likes, such as a bigger size, a shorter length, or leaving the edges out. If she still insists, you may decline that part of the service. Write on her card what you advised and what was agreed. A stylist who says no to damage keeps clients for years, because their hair stays healthy.

blocks.title: Children and consent
blocks.text: For a child, the parent or guardian agrees to the style, the time and the price, and must say whether photos may be taken. Never post a child's photo, or any client's face, without clear permission recorded on the card.

Before you start, read the key points back to her: "Medium knotless, mid-back, temples without added hair, about nine and a half hours, this price, your deposit received, no photos of your face." Ask her to reply "agreed" on WhatsApp if you booked there. That one message is your record if there is ever a dispute.

takeaways: Use a written card for every client and every visit.
Ask about the occasion, wear time, routine, picture and past pain.
Match the style to the assessment, not only to the photo.
Quote time from your own timed averages and write it down.
Record photo consent, and parent consent for children.

activity.title: Two practice consultations
steps: Prepare a blank record card with all eight fields.
Hold a role-play consultation with a friend who brings a style photo.
Complete the assessment and card, and calculate the time from your practice timings.
Read the agreement back and ask her to confirm in a WhatsApp message.
Repeat with a second person whose hair is different.
activity.evidence: Two completed record cards and screenshots of the two "agreed" messages (with names covered)

quiz.q: When you make a crown parting on dry hair, the scalp shows clearly along the part but is not visible elsewhere. What is the density at the crown?
options: Medium
High
Low
You cannot tell without washing
quiz.explain: A clear line of scalp along the part, with scalp hidden elsewhere, is medium density. Low density shows scalp even before parting.

quiz.q: A client's shed strand looks thinner than sewing thread and her temples are sparse. She wants tiny waist-length braids. What is the best advice?
options: Do exactly what she asks, it is her choice
Suggest medium braids at a shorter length with little or no added hair at the temples
Use extra tension at the temples so the braids last longer
Refuse to braid her hair at all
quiz.explain: Fine hair and thin edges cannot safely carry many small heavy braids. Bigger sections, shorter length and no added weight at the temples protect her hair.

quiz.q: During the scalp check you see round scaly patches with broken hairs on a child's scalp. What should you do?
options: Braid loosely over the patches
Apply an antifungal cream you have at home
Postpone the service, explain privately and suggest a clinic
Tell the other clients so they can avoid the child
quiz.explain: This may be ringworm of the scalp, which can spread on combs and towels. Postpone, refer privately, never treat or diagnose.

quiz.q: Which statement about head lice is correct according to the CDC?
options: They jump from head to head
They fly short distances
They live for weeks on salon chairs
They spread mainly through direct hair contact and also via shared combs and towels
quiz.explain: Lice crawl; they cannot hop or fly. They spread mainly by hair contact and also by shared combs, brushes and towels. Adults usually die within two days off the head.

quiz.q: A style needs 9 rows with an average of 8 braids per row. Your timed average is 5 minutes per braid. How long is the braiding?
options: 6 hours
5 hours
7 hours 12 minutes
4 hours 30 minutes
quiz.explain: 9 x 8 = 72 braids. 72 x 5 = 360 minutes, which is 6 hours. Add washing and drying on top.

modules.title: Wash, Condition and Prep Hair for Braiding
modules.overview: Neat, long-lasting braids start with clean, conditioned, detangled and stretched hair. This module turns washing and prepping into a timed salon service you can deliver with or without a basin, with methods that protect the hair and the client's comfort.

lessons.title: The salon wash service, with or without a basin
objectives: Set up a safe two-bucket wash station where there is no salon basin
Wash coily hair in sections so it tangles less
Cleanse the scalp and condition the length following dermatologist advice
Cost the products and water used in one wash

blocks.text: Many home salons in Nigeria have no backwash basin and no constant running water. That does not stop you giving a clean, comfortable, professional wash. What matters is the order of steps, the water temperature, washing in sections, and protecting the client's clothes, eyes and neck. This lesson sets up the service so it takes about 30 minutes and leaves hair ready to condition and stretch.

blocks.name: bucket
blocks.caption: Two buckets and a jug can give a clean, comfortable wash where there is no basin.

blocks.text: Setting up a two-bucket station

items: **Bucket A (clean water):** fill it with lukewarm water. Mix hot water into cold, never the other way round, and test it on the inside of your wrist. It should feel comfortably warm, not hot.
**Bucket B (used water):** placed under the client's head or beside the chair to catch rinse water.
**A jug or cup** for pouring, and a spray bottle for small sections.
**A cape or large plastic sheet**, a neck towel, and a dry towel for blotting.
**Shampoo, conditioner and a wide-tooth comb** within reach, so you never leave her with wet hair to fetch things.
**A low stool** so the client can lean forward over Bucket B, or a chair with a neck rest if she prefers to lean back.

blocks.title: Hot water and electricity
blocks.text: If you heat water with an electric kettle or immersion heater, do it away from the wash area and never with wet hands. Keep cables away from water and from the client's feet. Always mix and test water before it touches her head, and be extra careful with children.
Wash in sections

Coily hair tangles when it is rubbed loose in one big mass. Before wetting, divide the hair into four to six sections and twist or loosely band each one. You wash and rinse one section at a time while the others stay in place. The hair stays organised, tangles much less, and detangling later is faster.
The wash step by step

items: Seat the client, put on the cape and neck towel, and ask her to hold a small towel over her eyes.
Wet one section thoroughly with the jug, letting the water run into Bucket B.

Apply a small amount of shampoo to the scalp only. The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) advises massaging shampoo gently into the scalp and letting it flow through the length, rather than rubbing the length.
Use the pads of your fingers, never your nails, to work along the scalp.
Rinse until the water runs clear, then twist the section back and move to the next one.
Apply conditioner to the length of each section. The AAD advises using conditioner after every shampoo.
Rinse, then wrap the hair in a towel to absorb water. Do not rub it, which the AAD lists as a damaging habit.

blocks.title: The sectioned wash
items: Section and twist dry hair
Wet one section
Shampoo the scalp only
Rinse until clear
Condition the length
Wrap in towel, no rubbing
blocks.caption: Working section by section keeps coily hair organised from the first drop of water to the towel.

blocks.text: Common wash mistakes to avoid

items: **Piling all the hair on top of the head** and scrubbing it in circles. This creates knots that take longer to undo than the wash itself.
**Using too much shampoo.** A small amount on the scalp is enough; extra product is wasted money and takes longer to rinse.
**Leaving product in the hair.** Rinse each section until the water runs clear and the hair no longer feels slippery with shampoo. Leftover product can leave the scalp itchy under braids.
**Forgetting the ears and neck.** Wipe away water and foam from behind the ears and the hairline before she sits up, and change the neck towel if it is wet.

blocks.title: Worked example: what one wash costs
blocks.context: For example, Bisi runs a home salon in Ibadan and wants to know what to add to her price for a wash service. Prices here are approximate and change often.
steps: Shampoo: a 500 ml bottle costs about ₦4,500. One wash uses about 20 ml. Cost: 20 ÷ 500 x 4,500 = ₦180.
Conditioner: a 500 ml bottle costs about ₦5,000. One wash uses about 30 ml. Cost: 30 ÷ 500 x 5,000 = ₦300.
Water: two 25-litre jerrycans at about ₦100 each from a vendor: 2 x 100 = ₦200.
Total materials per wash: 180 + 300 + 200 = ₦680.
The service takes about 30 minutes of her time, which she will price separately in Module 4.
blocks.result: Bisi knows each wash costs her about ₦680 in materials before her time. She measures her actual usage for a week with a marked cup to check the 20 ml and 30 ml figures.

blocks.text: Drying before braiding

Hair must be fully dry before braiding with extensions. Damp hair sealed inside braids dries very slowly and can become unpleasant to wear. Low-porosity hair, which you identified in Module 1, takes the longest to dry, so book extra time for it. You will learn to dry and stretch hair at the same time in the next lesson.

blocks.title: Client comfort
blocks.text: Ask "Is the water okay?" after the first pour and "Is your neck comfortable?" halfway. A client leaning forward for 30 minutes gets tired; let her sit up between sections.

takeaways: Mix hot into cold water and test it on your wrist before it touches the head.
Section and twist the hair before wetting to reduce tangles.
Shampoo the scalp, condition the length, and blot with a towel, never rub.
A wash has a real material cost; measure it and include it in your price.
Hair must be fully dry before braiding with extensions.

steps: Set up the two-bucket station with all items within reach before the client sits down.
Section the hair into four to six twists and wash one section at a time.
Time the full service from cape on to towel wrap.
