lessons.title: Conditioning and stretching hair for neat parts
objectives: Deliver a deep conditioning step that follows the product label
Choose between heat and heatless stretching for each client
Blow-dry safely on the lowest effective heat
Use African threading as a heatless stretch and plan the timing

blocks.text: Tightly coiled hair shrinks as it dries. Shrunken hair is hard to part cleanly and hard to braid smoothly, so most stylists stretch the hair before braiding or twisting. You can stretch with heat or without heat. Both work. The right choice depends on the client's hair, her time and the style. This lesson also shows you how to add a deep conditioning step as a paid extra.

blocks.name: lotion-bottle
blocks.caption: Conditioning before you stretch makes the hair softer, easier to part and less likely to break.

blocks.text: Deep conditioning in a salon service

A deep conditioner (also called a hair mask or treatment) is thicker than a rinse-out conditioner and stays on longer. After shampooing, apply it section by section from the length to the ends, cover the hair with a plastic cap, and leave it for the time written on the label. Some products say to use gentle warmth from a hooded dryer or a warm towel; others do not. Follow the label, not a guess, and never leave a product on longer than it says. Rinse with lukewarm water until the hair no longer feels slippery with product.
Heat or heatless stretching?

head: Method
How it works
Time on the day
Best for
rows: Warm air dries and stretches each section
Wrapping each section with thread holds it stretched as it dries
Threads go in the evening before; removal takes minutes
Fine or fragile hair, clients avoiding heat
Soft hair ties placed down a section stretch it while it dries
Clients who can wait or return
Hair dries in big plaits and is stretched when undone
Clients who can prepare at home

blocks.text: Blow-drying safely

The AAD advises letting hair air dry when possible and using the lowest heat setting when you do use a dryer. Apply a heat protectant to each section, keep the dryer moving, and point the air down the hair shaft from root to ends. Work on hair that is damp, not dripping, so you spend less time under heat. Stop and check the client's scalp and ears are not getting hot. If the hair smells burnt or the ends feel crispy, the heat is too high.
African threading as a stretch

items: On damp, conditioned hair, make a section about the width of two fingers.
Hold the section at the root and tie the end of a soft thread or wool around its base, not tight on the scalp.
Wrap the thread down the section in close spirals, keeping the hair taut but not pulling the scalp.
Stop just before the ends, tuck the thread under the last wrap, and leave the tips free.
Leave the threads in until the hair is completely dry, usually overnight, then unwind them gently.

blocks.title: Heat stretch or heatless stretch
items: Blow-dry on low heat
Threading or banding
blocks.caption: Choose by the client's hair, her time and how much heat her hair can tolerate.

blocks.text: Checking the hair is ready

Before you start braiding, test that the hair is fully dry and evenly stretched. Feel the roots at the nape and behind the ears, where hair dries last. If the roots feel cool or damp, dry that area again before parting. Look at the ends: if they are split, thin or tangled into small knots, offer to trim only the damaged tips with clean, sharp hair scissors, and only with her agreement. Smooth, even ends make neater braids and a cleaner finish.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a stretch around the client's day
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi in Abuja has a client with fine, low-porosity hair who wants braids starting at 9 a.m. on Saturday.
steps: Option A, all on Saturday: wash 30 minutes + deep condition 20 minutes + blow-dry 45 minutes = 95 minutes before braiding starts. Braiding begins at about 10:35 a.m.
Option B, Friday evening: wash 30 minutes + deep condition 20 minutes + threading 40 minutes = 90 minutes on Friday.
On Saturday morning in Option B, removing threads takes about 10 minutes, so braiding begins at about 9:10 a.m.
Saturday time saved with Option B: 95 minus 10 = 85 minutes, and the fine hair gets no heat.
Ngozi offers Option B and charges for the Friday visit as a separate prep service.
blocks.result: The client sits for almost an hour and a half less on Saturday, her fine hair avoids heat, and Ngozi earns a separate prep fee for the Friday session.

blocks.title: Thread and pressure
blocks.text: Threading for stretching must not pull the scalp. If the client feels tightness at the root, unwind and re-wrap that section more loosely. Tension at the root is the same risk whether the hair is braided, threaded or twisted.

takeaways: Stretch hair before braiding so parts are clean and braids are smooth.
Follow the deep conditioner's label for time and heat.
Use the lowest heat setting that works, with a heat protectant.
Threading stretches hair without heat but needs drying time.
Plan the stretch around the client's day and price prep as its own service.

activity.title: Compare two stretch methods
steps: On a practice head, wash and condition the hair.
Blow-dry one half on low heat with a heat protectant, timing how long it takes.
Thread the other half for a heatless stretch and leave it to dry overnight.
Next day, compare the two halves for length, smoothness and how easily you can part them.
Write which method you would offer to a client with fine hair and why.
activity.evidence: Photos of both halves, your timings and your written recommendation

lessons.title: Detangling in the chair: technique, takedown and tender heads
objectives: Detangle coily hair from the ends up without pulling the scalp
Tell normal shedding apart from breakage after a takedown
Keep a tender-headed client, including a child, calm and comfortable
Time and price detangling and takedown as separate services

blocks.text: Detangling is where most damage happens in a salon, because it is slow and stylists get impatient. Pulling a comb from the roots through a knot breaks strands and hurts the client. The professional method is the opposite: small sections, plenty of slip, start at the ends and work up, and always hold the hair so the pull never reaches the scalp.

blocks.name: hourglass
blocks.caption: Detangling cannot be rushed. Patience here saves breakage you would see for months.

blocks.text: The detangling method

items: Work on damp hair with a conditioner or detangling product that gives slip. The AAD advises combing textured hair while it is damp, with a wide-tooth comb.
Take a section no wider than your palm. Clip the rest away.
Gently separate the section with your fingers first, feeling for knots and shed hair.
Hold the section firmly a little above where you are combing, so the comb pulls against your hand and not against the scalp.
Comb the last few centimetres of the ends first. When they are smooth, move up a little and comb down through the ends again.
Continue upward until the comb glides from root to tip. Twist the finished section and move on.

blocks.title: One detangling pass
items: Small damp section
Add slip product
Fingers first
Hold above, comb ends
Work upward slowly
Twist and clip away
blocks.caption: Every section follows the same pass, from ends to roots, with your hand absorbing the pull.

blocks.text: After a takedown: shed hair is normal

The AAD notes that it is normal to shed about 50 to 100 hairs a day. While hair is braided, shed hairs cannot fall out, so they stay trapped inside the braid. When braids come out after several weeks, clients are often shocked by the amount of loose hair. Explain this calmly. A shed hair usually has a small white bulb at one end. Short broken pieces without a bulb are breakage, which is worth noting on her card, especially if most of it comes from the edges or one area.

After a takedown, remove the shed hair and the buildup at the base of each section with your fingers before you wet it. Water makes trapped shed hair mat into knots. Separate, finger-detangle, then wash.
Tender heads and children

items: Tell the client what you are about to do, and ask her to say "stop" if anything hurts.
Keep sections small. A small section is less painful than a big one.
Hold above the knot every time, so she feels the comb and not a pull.
With children, allow short breaks, talk to them, and let them hold a mirror or a toy.
Never hold a child down or rush because the parent is in a hurry. Book more time instead.

blocks.text: Tools and common mistakes

head: Tool
Use it for
Avoid
rows: First pass on every section, feeling for knots
Rushing this step to save time
Re-dampening hair that dries while you work
Detangling hair that has dried and shrunk
Holding finished and waiting sections apart

blocks.text: The commonest mistake is detangling a section that has dried while you were working on another. Dry, shrunken coils grip each other and snap. Keep the spray bottle at hand and re-dampen as you go. The second mistake is taking sections that are too big because the client is in a hurry. Bigger sections hurt more and break more hair, so they rarely save any real time.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing takedown and detangling
blocks.context: For example, Kemi in Port Harcourt gets many clients who arrive with old braids still in. She used to do takedown and detangling free and her days ran late.
steps: She times herself on five clients. Takedown of medium box braids averages 75 minutes, and detangling before washing averages 45 minutes.
Total extra time per client: 75 + 45 = 120 minutes, which is 2 hours.
Her target for her own time is about ₦1,500 per hour (approximate, set from her own budget). 2 x 1,500 = ₦3,000.
She adds a small amount for detangling product used, about ₦200, giving ₦3,000 + ₦200 = ₦3,200.
She lists "Takedown and detangle, medium braids: ₦3,200" on her price menu and tells clients they can save this by removing braids at home.
blocks.result: Kemi's long days now pay for themselves, and clients understand why arriving with braids in costs more and takes longer.

blocks.title: Scissors last, not first
blocks.text: If a knot will not open after patient finger work, ask before you cut. Cutting is sometimes the kind choice for a tight matted knot at the ends, but the client should agree first, and you should note it on her card.

takeaways: Detangle damp hair, in small sections, from the ends up.
Hold the hair above where you comb so the scalp is never pulled.
Shed hair with a white bulb is normal after a takedown; short pieces without a bulb are breakage.
Remove shed hair before wetting a takedown, or it mats.
Time takedown and detangling and price them as services.

activity.title: Detangling practice and timing
steps: Detangle a practice head or a willing family member using the full method.
Count how many sections you used and time each one.
Collect the loose hair on a white cloth and sort it into shed hair (with a bulb) and broken pieces.
Write the total time and your suggested price for this service using your own hourly target.
Ask your practice client to rate comfort from 1 to 5 and note what you would change.
activity.evidence: Your time log, a photo of the sorted hair, and your comfort score and notes

quiz.q: There is no basin. Which set-up is safest for a wash service?
options: Pour water from a kettle straight onto the scalp
Mix hot water into cold in a clean bucket, test it on your wrist, and rinse into a second bucket
Wash the hair in the same bucket it rinses into
Use cold water only so you never need to test it
quiz.explain: Two buckets keep clean and used water separate, and testing mixed water on your wrist prevents scalds.

quiz.q: According to AAD advice used in this module, what is the correct way to shampoo?
options: Rub shampoo hard along the full length
Apply shampoo only to the ends
Massage shampoo into the scalp and let it flow through the length
Skip conditioner if you used good shampoo
quiz.explain: The AAD advises massaging shampoo into the scalp, letting it flow through the length, and using conditioner after every shampoo.

quiz.q: A client with fine hair wants braids early tomorrow and prefers no heat. Which plan fits best?
options: Blow-dry on high heat tomorrow to save time
Braid her hair while it is still wet
Skip stretching completely
Wash, condition and thread her hair this evening so it dries stretched overnight
quiz.explain: Threading the evening before stretches the hair without heat and leaves it dry for an early start.

quiz.q: After a takedown, the client finds many loose hairs, most with a small white bulb at one end. What is the best explanation?
options: These are mostly normal shed hairs that were trapped inside the braids
She is losing her hair and must see a doctor at once
The braids caused all of this breakage
The shampoo made her hair fall out
quiz.explain: Shed hairs have a bulb and are normal; they collect inside braids. Short pieces without a bulb would be breakage to note on her card.

quiz.q: Takedown takes you 60 minutes and detangling 30 minutes. Your time target is ₦1,600 per hour and product costs ₦200. What do you charge?

modules.title: Braiding and Twisting Techniques for Clients
modules.overview: This module moves from practice to client-ready technique: precise parting grids and flat twists, knotless feed-in braids and traditional African threading, and feed-in cornrows done with tension that protects the hairline. Every technique is taught with the time, materials and safety checks a paid service needs.

lessons.title: Parting grids, brick-lay patterns and flat twists
objectives: Part clean, even sections in a square grid and a brick-lay pattern
Count braids from a parting plan and estimate the time
Install neat flat twists on natural hair without extensions
Check parting quality with a hand mirror and a phone photo

blocks.text: Clients judge a braid style first by its parts. Straight, even parts make even cheap extension hair look expensive. Crooked, uneven parts make a style look rushed, and uneven sections also carry uneven weight, which strains the smaller ones. This lesson teaches the two parting patterns used for most box braids and twists, how to count braids before you start, and a quick natural-hair style, flat twists, that you can offer at a lower price.

blocks.name: haircut-female-sign
blocks.alt: A woman having her hair styled
blocks.caption: Clean parts are the first thing a client notices in the mirror.

blocks.text: Tools for parting

items: A rat-tail (tail) comb with a fine, firm tail for drawing lines.
Six to ten clips to hold hair away from the working row.
A spray bottle and a light styling gel or cream to smooth the edges of each section.
A hand mirror, plus your phone camera to check the back of the head from a distance.

blocks.text: Square grid and brick-lay

In a **square grid**, every row is divided at the same points, so the parts form straight lines from front to back like a chessboard. It looks very neat when the hair is tied up, but straight channels of scalp show when braids fall loose. In a **brick-lay** pattern, each row is shifted by half a section, like bricks in a wall. The parts of one row sit behind the middle of the braids in the row above, so the scalp is covered better when the braids hang down. Brick-lay usually means one row has one braid fewer than the next.

blocks.title: Square grid or brick-lay
items: Square grid
Brick-lay
left: Parts line up front to back
right: Each row shifted half a section
Takes a little longer to plan
blocks.caption: Choose the pattern with the client: how she will wear her braids decides which looks better.

blocks.text: Parting step by step

items: Start at the nape. Draw the first horizontal row about the height you want each section to be, and clip all hair above it away.
Divide the row into equal sections. Use your fingers or the comb's teeth as a ruler so each section is the same width.
Smooth each section with a little product so stray hairs do not cross into the next part.
Braid or twist the whole row before parting the next, so you always work from a clean line.
For brick-lay, start the next row's first part in the middle of the section below it.
After every two rows, take a phone photo from behind and check that sizes are even.

blocks.title: Worked example: counting a brick-lay plan
blocks.context: For example, Aisha in Kano plans medium box braids in brick-lay for a client and wants to quote the time.
steps: She maps 8 rows from nape to front.
Rows 1, 3, 5 and 7 hold 10 braids each: 4 x 10 = 40 braids.
Rows 2, 4, 6 and 8 are shifted half a section and hold 9 braids each: 4 x 9 = 36 braids.
Total: 40 + 36 = 76 braids.
Her timed average for medium box braids is 6 minutes each: 76 x 6 = 456 minutes, which is 7 hours 36 minutes of braiding.
blocks.result: Aisha quotes about 7 hours 40 minutes of braiding, plus prep time, and buys extension hair for 76 braids instead of guessing.

blocks.text: Flat twists on natural hair

A flat twist lies flat against the scalp like a cornrow, but it uses two strands twisted over each other instead of three braided. It needs no extension hair, takes less time, and suits clients who want a lighter, cheaper style or a protective style between braid installations.

items: Part a straight row from the front hairline towards the nape, about two to three fingers wide. Clip the rest away.
At the front, take two small strands from the section.
Cross the right strand over the left, then pick up a little loose hair from the section and add it to the strand that is now on the right.
Repeat: cross, pick up, add, keeping the twist flat on the scalp and the tension gentle.
When the section ends, continue as a two-strand twist to the ends and coil the tip around your finger.

blocks.text: For example, six flat twists at about 12 minutes each take 6 x 12 = 72 minutes, a quick service you can fit between longer bookings. Clients can wear them as a style, or unravel them after a few days for a stretched twist-out.

Three parting problems cause most redos. Sections that grow bigger towards the front happen when you stop measuring with your fingers as you get tired, so check the size against the first row. Parts that drift sideways happen when the client tilts her head; ask her to keep her chin level and look straight ahead. Fuzzy parts happen on dry hair, so lightly mist and smooth each row before you draw the line.

blocks.title: Practise on a mannequin head
blocks.text: Partings improve fastest with repetition. If you can, practise on a training mannequin head and photograph every attempt from behind. Compare your first and fifth photos: the difference keeps you motivated.

takeaways: Even parts mean even weight on each section, not only a better look.
Square grid lines up; brick-lay shifts each row by half a section for better scalp cover.
Count rows and braids before you start, and use the count to quote time and hair.
Flat twists are a quick natural-hair service with no extensions.
Check your parts with a phone photo from behind every two rows.

activity.title: Part and count a full head
steps: On a practice head, part the back half in a square grid and the front half in brick-lay.
Count the braids or twists you would need for the whole head in each pattern.
Time yourself parting and twisting three sections and work out your minutes per section.
Photograph the finished parting from behind.
Install six flat twists on another practice head and time the full style.
activity.evidence: Photos of both parting patterns, your braid count, and your time per section

lessons.title: Knotless feed-in braids and African threading styles
objectives: Start and build a knotless braid by feeding in extension hair gradually
Prepare and count feed-in pieces before a service
Install a traditional African threading style safely
Finish braid ends safely, protecting the client from heat

blocks.text: Knotless braids are among the most requested braid styles because they look natural at the root and put less sudden weight on the scalp at the start of each braid. African threading, known in Yoruba as **irun kiko**, is one of the oldest Nigerian styling methods, using thread wrapped around sections of natural hair. One is a modern extension style; the other needs no extensions at all. Offering both widens your menu and your price range.

blocks.name: knot
blocks.caption: Knotless braids avoid the knot of added hair at the root by feeding extensions in gradually.

blocks.text: How a knotless braid is built

In a traditional box braid, a folded piece of extension hair is looped around the base of the section, so the braid starts with added weight and a small bump of extension hair at the root. In a knotless braid, you start braiding the client's own hair alone for a few stitches, then add very small pieces of extension hair one at a time as you braid down. The root looks like her own hair, and the weight builds gradually.

items: Part a clean section and smooth it with a little product. Divide the section's own hair into three strands.
Braid two or three stitches with her hair only, keeping the tension firm but painless.
Lay a thin feed-in piece of extension hair, folded in half, over the braid so each half joins a side strand.
Braid two or three more stitches, then add the next feed-in piece the same way.
Continue adding pieces until the braid reaches the thickness you agreed, then braid to the end without adding more.
Run your fingers down the braid to check that no extension hair is poking out, and that the root does not tug when the client turns her head.

blocks.title: Building one knotless braid
items: Braid own hair first
Add thin feed-in piece
Braid a few stitches
Add next piece
Braid to the end
Check root and finish
blocks.caption: Weight is added little by little, so the root carries her own hair, not a heavy loop.

blocks.text: Preparing extension hair

Prepare all your feed-in pieces before the client sits down. Pre-stretched braiding hair saves time because the ends are already tapered. Split each pack into pieces of a consistent size, roughly the same thickness each time, and lay them in labelled piles. Count the pieces you need from your braid plan, not by guesswork.

blocks.title: Worked example: counting feed-in pieces and packs
blocks.context: For example, Tola in Lagos plans 60 medium knotless braids and adds 3 feed-in pieces to each braid.
steps: Pieces needed: 60 braids x 3 pieces = 180 pieces.
From practice, she knows she gets about 30 pieces of this size from one pack.
Packs needed: 180 ÷ 30 = 6 packs. She buys one spare pack, so 7 packs.
At about ₦1,200 per pack (an approximate local price), 7 x 1,200 = ₦8,400.
She tells the client the hair cost in advance and writes "7 packs, ₦8,400" on the record card.
blocks.result: Tola arrives with the right amount of hair, prepared in even piles, and the client sees exactly where the hair money went.

blocks.text: Finishing the ends safely

Many stylists dip synthetic braid ends in hot water to seal and smooth them. Hot water burns quickly. Ask the client to stand or lean away, protect her neck and shoulders with a towel, hold the cup or flask yourself well below her shoulders, and dip only the ends. Never pour hot water over braids still on her head near the skin. Synthetic hair can also catch fire, so never use a lighter or open flame near a client's head.

blocks.title: Heat near the client
blocks.text: Keep the kettle and flask on a stable surface away from children and walkways. Water that has just boiled can scald in a second. If skin is burned, cool it under clean running water and seek medical help for anything more than a small, mild burn.
African threading (irun kiko)

items: On clean, stretched, moisturised hair, part the sections for the chosen design, often a crown of upright or curved threaded stems.
Use a soft black thread or wool. Tie it at the base of the section without pulling the scalp.
Wrap the thread down the section in tight, even spirals so the hair is completely covered, like a smooth cord.
Bend or join the threaded stems into the design: curves, arches, or bunches meeting at the crown.
Secure the ends by tucking the thread under the last wraps.

blocks.text: Threading is light because it adds no extension hair, and it stretches the hair as it holds the style. The tension risk is at the base: if the thread is tied tightly against the scalp, or if many stems are pulled to one point, the hairline is strained. Leave a little slack at the base of every section and ask the client how it feels before you move on.

takeaways: Knotless braids start with her own hair and add extension weight gradually.
Count feed-in pieces and packs from your braid plan before the service.
Sealing ends with hot water needs a towel, distance and steady hands; no open flame.
African threading adds no extension weight but still needs slack at the base.
Write hair quantity and cost on the record card.

activity.title: Knotless and threading practice
steps: Prepare 30 feed-in pieces from one pack and lay them in even piles.
Install ten knotless braids on a practice head, timing each one.
Check every root for a tug and every braid for poking hairs; redo any that fail.
Thread a simple design of six stems on another practice head.
Photograph both and write your average time per knotless braid.
activity.evidence: Photos of your feed-in piles, knotless braids and threading design, plus your timing note

lessons.title: Feed-in cornrows with safe tension: preventing traction alopecia
objectives: Install a feed-in cornrow that starts thin and builds gradually
Recognise signs of too much tension during and after a service
Apply a tension check routine at the hairline and every row
Advise clients on wear time and rest using dermatologist guidance

blocks.text: Traction alopecia is hair loss caused by repeated pulling on the hair, usually from tight braids, cornrows, ponytails, weaves and extensions. It often starts at the temples and hairline, the same places where hair is thinnest. Long-term pulling can lead to permanent hair loss. As a stylist you can prevent much of it, with technique, with honesty and with the advice you give. This lesson teaches feed-in cornrows, a style where tension control is especially important.

blocks.name: warning-sign
blocks.caption: Pain during braiding is a warning, not a sign the style will last longer.

blocks.text: Feed-in cornrows step by step

items: Part a clean row from the hairline towards the nape. Leave the finest baby hairs at the front out of the cornrow.
Start braiding with her own hair only for the first few stitches, using an underhand or overhand cornrow stitch.
Add a very thin piece of extension hair to a side strand, braid two or three stitches, and add another thin piece.
Keep adding thin pieces until the row reaches the agreed thickness. The row should look thin at the front and fuller at the back.
Braid off the scalp to the end of the extension hair and finish the end.

blocks.text: Feed-in cornrows look natural at the front because they start thin. That also protects her hairline, because the first stitches carry no extension weight. Never start a cornrow with a thick piece of added hair at the hairline.
Signs that tension is too high

head: When
Sign
What you do
rows: She winces, holds her head, or says it hurts
Stop. Undo and redo that section more loosely.
Skin lifts in little tents at the base of the braid
Redo the braid. The scalp should lie flat.
Redness around many braid bases, or she cannot move her eyebrows or turn her head comfortably
Loosen or redo the tightest rows before she leaves.
Small bumps or spots at the base of braids, soreness
Advise her to have the tight braids removed. Refer to a health worker if there is pus or the soreness grows.
Thinning at the temples or a receding hairline
No tension at the hairline. Suggest a health worker or dermatologist.

blocks.title: Tension check at every service
items: Ask about past pain
Hairline left free
No scalp tenting
No pain on any row
Wear time agreed
blocks.caption: Run this check at the start, during every row, and before she leaves the chair.

blocks.text: What dermatologists advise

items: The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) lists tight ponytails, buns and cornrows among habits that damage hair, and advises wearing hair loosely pulled back.
For weaves and hair extensions, the AAD advises keeping them in for 2 or 3 months at most.
The AAD also advises keeping the scalp clean and alternating hairstyles, rather than always using the same tight style.

blocks.text: Put these into everyday words for your clients: "If it hurts, it is too tight. Tell me and I will redo it. Take these out by this date. After this style, give your hair a lighter style or a rest before we braid again." Write the agreed takedown date on her card and send her a WhatsApp reminder a week before.

blocks.title: Worked example: a client returns with bumps
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Benin City braided feed-in cornrows with extensions for a client on 3 March. The client returns on 12 May asking for the same style again.
steps: Grace counts the time: from 3 March to 12 May is 70 days, which is 70 ÷ 7 = 10 weeks, inside the AAD's 2 to 3 month limit but near its end.
During the scalp check she sees small bumps along the front hairline and the client says the front has felt sore for a week.
She removes the old cornrows gently, finger-detangling each one, and does not re-braid the hairline today.
She advises the client to see a health worker if the bumps have pus or get worse, and writes what she saw on the card.
She offers a low-tension style for now: large two-strand twists on her own hair, with the hairline left completely free, and a takedown reminder in four weeks.
blocks.result: The client leaves with a style that rests her hairline, a clear plan, and trust that Grace will not damage her hair for the sake of a sale.

blocks.title: Heavy hair and small sections
blocks.text: Weight is tension too. Very long or thick extensions on very small sections pull on the roots all day, every day, even when the braid was not braided tightly. Match extension length and thickness to the section size and her hair density.

Children need extra care. Their hairlines are delicate, and parents often ask for very tight styles so they last through the school term. Explain that tight styles can harm a child's edges, offer bigger sections with no extensions at the hairline, and suggest a takedown date that suits school holidays. A child should never leave your chair in pain.

takeaways: Traction alopecia comes from repeated pulling; long-term pulling can make hair loss permanent.
Feed-in cornrows start with her own hair and add thin pieces gradually.
Pain, scalp tenting and bumps mean the style is too tight; stop and redo.
The AAD advises extensions for 2 or 3 months at most and alternating styles.
Leave the hairline free and match extension weight to section size.

activity.title: Feed-in cornrows with a tension log
steps: Install four feed-in cornrows on a practice head or a willing client.
After each row, ask for a comfort score from 1 (very tight) to 5 (comfortable) and record it.
Redo any row scoring below 4 and record the new score.
Write a takedown date for the style using the AAD's 2 to 3 month guidance.
Draft the WhatsApp reminder you would send one week before takedown.
activity.evidence: Photos of the cornrows, your tension log with scores, and your reminder message

quiz.q: A client wears her braids loose, hanging down, and dislikes seeing straight lines of scalp. Which parting pattern suits her best?
options: Square grid
One large section
Brick-lay
Random parts
quiz.explain: Brick-lay shifts each row by half a section so parts do not line up, giving better scalp cover when braids hang down.

quiz.q: A brick-lay plan has 6 rows: three rows of 12 braids and three rows of 11 braids. How many braids is that?
What makes a knotless braid different from a traditional box braid?
options: It starts with her own hair and adds small extension pieces gradually
It uses no extension hair at all
It is always braided tighter
It is only done on relaxed hair
quiz.explain: A knotless braid begins with her own hair and feeds in thin pieces as it goes, so there is no heavy loop at the root.

quiz.q: While you braid, the skin at the base of a cornrow lifts into a little tent. What should you do?
options: Continue; it will relax in a day
Undo and redo that section with less tension
Give her a painkiller
Spray water on it
quiz.explain: Tenting shows the braid is pulling the scalp. Redo it more loosely. Never offer medicines; that is outside your role.

quiz.q: Which advice on wear time follows the AAD guidance used in this module?
options: Keep extensions in as long as they look neat
Remove all braids after one week
Keep weaves and extensions in for 2 or 3 months at most and alternate styles
Re-braid only the edges every month and keep the rest
quiz.explain: The AAD advises keeping weaves and extensions in for 2 or 3 months at most, keeping the scalp clean, and alternating styles.

modules.title: Hygiene, Timing and Pricing Your Services
modules.overview: A skilled stylist still loses clients if her tools are dirty, her days run late or her prices do not cover her costs. This module gives you a between-client hygiene reset based on WHO and CDC guidance, a timing system for booking realistic days, and a pricing method that turns your service menu into steady income.

lessons.title: Hygiene between clients: the 15-minute reset
objectives: Clean and then disinfect tools and surfaces in the correct order
Mix a 0.1% bleach solution accurately from the strength on the label
Handle towels, capes and hair waste so nothing passes between clients
Wash hands correctly before and after every client

blocks.text: Combs, clips, towels and capes move from head to head all day. Without a routine, they can carry lice, fungal infections and bacteria from one client to the next. A clean salon is also something clients notice and talk about. This lesson builds a reset routine you do after every single client, which takes about 15 minutes once you are used to it, plus a deeper clean at the end of each day.

blocks.name: wash-hands
blocks.caption: Clean hands at the start and end of every client are the cheapest protection in your salon.

blocks.text: Clean first, then disinfect

Cleaning removes hair, product and dirt with soap and water. Disinfecting kills germs that remain. You must clean first, because the World Health Organization (WHO) explains that surfaces must be cleaned with water and soap or a detergent to remove dirt before disinfection. A disinfectant poured over a comb full of hair and gel does very little.
Mixing a 0.1% bleach solution

WHO guidance for cleaning surfaces outside health facilities gives 0.1% sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) as a recommended concentration, which is 1 part of 5% household bleach to 49 parts of water. Bleach brands differ in strength, so read the percentage on your bottle. The general rule is: millilitres of bleach = 0.1 x total millilitres you want ÷ the bleach percentage on the label.

blocks.title: Worked example: mixing 2 litres of disinfectant
blocks.context: For example, Zainab in Jos wants 2 litres (2,000 ml) of 0.1% solution for her tool tray and surfaces.
steps: With 5% bleach: 0.1 x 2,000 ÷ 5 = 40 ml of bleach.
Water: 2,000 minus 40 = 1,960 ml. Check: 40 is 1 part and 1,960 is 49 parts, because 40 x 49 = 1,960.
With a bleach labelled 3.5%: 0.1 x 2,000 ÷ 3.5 = about 57 ml of bleach, and 2,000 minus 57 = 1,943 ml of water.
She measures the bleach with a marked measuring cup kept only for bleach, pours it into the water, and labels the container "0.1% bleach, do not drink" with the date.
She mixes it in a well-ventilated place, wearing rubber gloves, and makes a fresh batch each working day.
blocks.result: Zainab has a correctly diluted solution for any bleach brand, instead of the common guess of "a little splash" that may be too weak to work or strong enough to irritate skin.

blocks.title: Bleach safety
blocks.text: WHO warns never to combine disinfectants such as bleach and ammonia, because mixtures can release dangerous gases. Never mix bleach with other cleaners. Wear rubber gloves, open windows, keep bleach away from children and food, and rinse tools in clean water after disinfecting. Bleach can damage metal, so use it on plastic combs and surfaces, and wash metal tools well with soap and water instead.
The reset after every client

items: Sweep up hair and put it in a covered bin. Do not leave it on the floor for the next client to walk through.
Remove used combs and clips to a "used" container. Never put them back on the tray.
Wash them in soapy water, scrub between the teeth with a small brush, and rinse.
Soak plastic tools in the 0.1% solution for the time recommended on your bleach label, then rinse in clean water and dry.
Wipe the chair, armrests, tray and mirror with soapy water, then with the bleach solution.
Put the used towel and cape in the laundry bag and take out fresh ones.
Wash your hands, then set out clean tools from the covered "clean" container.

blocks.title: The between-client reset
items: Sweep and bin hair
Wash tools with soap
Disinfect, rinse, dry
Wipe chair and tray
Fresh towel and cape
Wash hands
blocks.caption: Run the same cycle after every client so clean and used items never mix.

blocks.text: Towels, capes and hands

items: **One towel per client.** Wash used towels and capes in hot water and dry them fully, ideally in the sun.
**After a client with lice,** the CDC advises soaking combs and brushes in hot water of at least about 54°C (130°F) for 5 to 10 minutes and washing linens on a hot cycle.
**Hand washing:** wash with soap and clean water for 40 to 60 seconds, covering palms, backs of hands, between fingers and under nails, before and after every client.
**Cuts on your hands:** cover them with a waterproof plaster, and wear gloves when working near any broken skin on a client.

blocks.text: The end-of-day deep clean

At closing time, empty and wash the tool containers themselves, not only the tools inside them. Wash brushes and the small scrubbing brush, and leave everything to dry fully before you close the containers, because damp, closed boxes grow mould. Wipe door handles, your phone and the payment card reader if you use one. Throw away any 0.1% solution left over: it should be made fresh each working day. Wash the day's towels and capes, and check your stock of gloves, soap and neck strips so you never start a day without them.

takeaways: Always clean with soap and water before you disinfect.
0.1% bleach is 1 part of 5% bleach to 49 parts water; adjust for your label's strength.
Never mix bleach with ammonia or other cleaners; ventilate and wear gloves.
Keep used and clean tools in separate containers.
One towel per client, and hands washed for 40 to 60 seconds before and after each one.

activity.title: Set up and time your reset
steps: Label two containers "clean" and "used" and a laundry bag for towels and capes.
Read your bleach label and calculate the amount for 1 litre of 0.1% solution.
Mix it safely with gloves and ventilation, and label the container with the date.
Run the full reset after a practice session and time it.
Write your reset steps on a card and stick it where you can see it.
activity.evidence: Your dilution calculation, a photo of your labelled containers, and your timed reset card

lessons.title: Timing services and planning a realistic booking day
objectives: Keep a timing log and calculate your average time per braid, row or service
Build a full service time from consultation to reset
Plan a day of bookings with resets and breaks that finishes on time
Use WhatsApp Business tools to confirm and remind clients

blocks.text: "It will take about three hours" turns into six, the next client waits, and everyone leaves unhappy. Late days come from guessing times instead of measuring them. In this lesson you build a timing log from your real work, use it to calculate service times, and plan days with space for hygiene resets and your own breaks.

blocks.name: stopwatch
blocks.caption: Your own measured times are the only reliable basis for bookings.

blocks.text: Your timing log

For the next ten services, write the start and end time of every stage: consultation, scalp check, wash, drying or stretching, parting and braiding, finishing, and reset. For braids, also count how many braids you did, so you can work out minutes per braid. After ten services, calculate your averages. Your speed will improve, so update the averages every month.

head: Stage
What you record
Example average
rows: Minutes and number of braids or rows

blocks.text: Building one service time

Service time = consultation + prep + (number of braids x your minutes per braid) + finishing. Then add the reset after the client leaves before you book the next one. For example, medium box braids with 76 braids at 6 minutes each need 456 minutes of braiding. With a second trained stylist working at the same speed on the other half of the head, braiding time falls to 456 ÷ 2 = 228 minutes, but the consultation, wash and finishing do not get shorter.

blocks.title: One client, start to reset
items: Consult and scalp check
Wash and condition
Dry and stretch
Part and braid
Finish and aftercare
15-minute reset
blocks.caption: Book the whole timeline, not only the braiding, or every later client starts late.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning a Saturday
blocks.context: For example, Blessing in Owerri has three Saturday bookings and wants to finish by 3 p.m. to collect her children.
steps: Booking 1, feed-in cornrows: from her log, 180 minutes in total, from 8:00 to 11:00. Reset 11:00 to 11:15.

Booking 2, six flat twists: 72 minutes of twisting plus 10 minutes consultation and 10 minutes finishing is 92 minutes. She books a 105-minute slot, leaving 13 minutes spare: 11:15 to 13:00. Reset 13:00 to 13:15.
Lunch for herself: 13:15 to 13:45.
Booking 3, a child's wash and detangle: 60 minutes, 13:45 to 14:45. Reset 14:45 to 15:00.
Check: 180 + 15 + 105 + 15 + 30 + 60 + 15 = 420 minutes, which is exactly 7 hours from 8:00, ending at 15:00.
blocks.result: Blessing's day includes every reset and a real lunch, has a small buffer in the middle, and ends on time. She declines a fourth request and offers it on Monday instead.

blocks.text: Confirming and reminding on WhatsApp

items: Use the WhatsApp Business app's **quick replies** for your booking confirmation, so every client gets the same clear details: date, start time, style, estimated hours, price, deposit and what to bring.
Use **labels** such as "Deposit paid", "Reminder sent" and "Takedown due" to see at a glance where each client stands.
Send a reminder the day before, asking her to arrive with hair detangled or to tell you if she needs takedown.
Set an **away message** for the hours when you are busy with a client, so new enquiries know when you will reply.

blocks.title: Protect your body too
blocks.text: Long braiding sessions strain your back, neck and wrists. Adjust the client's chair height so you work with relaxed shoulders, stand or stretch between rows, and drink water. A schedule that breaks your body is not sustainable.
Booking rules worth writing down

items: **Arrival:** tell clients how long you will wait before a booking is shortened or moved, for example 30 minutes.
**Prep:** say whether she must arrive with hair washed, detangled and free of old braids, or book those as add-ons.
**Children:** a parent or guardian stays, or remains reachable by phone, for the whole service.
**Rescheduling:** how much notice you need for a deposit to be carried forward.
**Busy periods:** around festive seasons and school resumption, open bookings early and stick to your daily limit rather than squeezing in extra clients.

blocks.text: Put these rules in your WhatsApp Business profile or a pinned message, and send them with every confirmation. Rules written in advance feel fair to clients; rules invented on the day feel like punishment.

If a client arrives late, start with what fits. Tell her honestly: "We have lost 40 minutes. I can finish at the size we agreed if you can stay later, or we can make the braids slightly bigger to finish on time." Let her choose and write it on the card.

takeaways: Measure every stage for ten services before you trust your times.
Service time includes consultation, prep, braiding, finishing and the reset.
A second stylist shortens braiding, not consultation or washing.
Plan the day in full, with resets, a break and a small buffer.
Use WhatsApp Business quick replies, labels and reminders for every booking.

activity.title: Ten-service timing log and a planned day
steps: Create a timing log table in a notebook or spreadsheet with the six stages.
Record every stage for your next services (aim for ten; practice heads count).
Calculate your average minutes per braid for one style.
Plan a realistic working day of three bookings using your averages, including resets and a break.
Write your WhatsApp booking confirmation as a quick reply.
activity.evidence: Your timing log, your averages, your planned day and a screenshot of your quick reply

lessons.title: Pricing services: a cost-based menu, deposits and safe payments
objectives: Calculate the full cost of a service from materials, time and overheads
Set a menu price with a profit margin and check it against your local market
Price add-ons and client-supplied hair fairly
Take deposits and payments safely by bank transfer

blocks.text: Many stylists copy the price of the salon down the road. That price may not cover their own hair packs, products, fuel and time. In this lesson you build a price from your own costs, add a profit margin, and only then compare with the market. You also set clear rules for deposits and payments so you are not left with unpaid work or fake transfer alerts.

blocks.name: pricing-page
blocks.alt: A price list with service options
blocks.caption: A clear menu built from your real costs makes pricing conversations short and confident.

blocks.text: The four parts of a service cost

items: **Materials:** extension hair, gel, mousse, conditioner, shampoo, and the wash cost you calculated in Module 2.
**Consumables:** neck strips, gloves, cotton, and the disinfectant you use in the reset.
**Your time:** the total hours from your timing log multiplied by your hourly target. Set the target from what you need to earn each month, divided by the hours you actually work.
**Overhead share:** monthly costs such as generator fuel, data, cleaning supplies, laundry and a share of rent, divided by the number of services you do in a month.

blocks.title: Building a service price
items: Add up materials
Add your time
Add overhead share
Add profit margin
Round, compare with market
blocks.caption: Build the price from your costs first; compare with other salons only at the end.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing feed-in cornrows
blocks.context: For example, Ifeoma in Asaba prices 8 feed-in cornrows with extensions, including a wash. All naira amounts are approximate.
steps: Materials and consumables: 3 packs of braiding hair at ₦1,200 = ₦3,600; gel and mousse ₦500; wash materials ₦680; gloves and neck strip ₦150. Total: 3,600 + 500 + 680 + 150 = ₦4,930.
Time: her log shows 3.5 hours in total. At her target of ₦1,500 per hour: 3.5 x 1,500 = ₦5,250.
Overhead share: monthly overheads of about ₦30,000 divided by about 60 services a month = ₦500.
Total cost: 4,930 + 5,250 + 500 = ₦10,680. With a 20% profit margin: 10,680 x 1.2 = ₦12,816, which she rounds to ₦13,000.
If the client brings her own hair: 10,680 minus 3,600 = ₦7,080, x 1.2 = ₦8,496, rounded to ₦8,500.
blocks.result: Ifeoma's menu shows feed-in cornrows at ₦13,000 with hair supplied, or ₦8,500 with the client's own hair. She checks that these sit within the range of nearby salons offering similar quality.

blocks.text: A clear price menu

head: Service
What is included
How it is priced
rows: Consultation, scalp check, style, finishing, aftercare advice
By size and length, with or without hair supplied
Blow-dry on low heat, or threading the day before
Fixed add-on, or a separate prep visit
By style size, from your timing log

blocks.text: Pricing size, length and add-ons

Size and length change both time and hair. Smaller braids mean more braids, so more minutes; longer braids mean more packs. Do not guess a percentage increase. Recalculate each version from your braid count and timing log. For example, if Ifeoma's medium knotless braids are 60 braids at 6 minutes, that is 360 minutes, and small knotless at 110 braids and 5 minutes each is 550 minutes. The small version needs 190 more minutes of her time, so its price must rise by at least 190 ÷ 60 x 1,500 = ₦4,750 for time alone, before extra hair.

items: **Discounts:** offer them on purpose, such as a small loyalty discount on every fifth visit, never because a client pushed hard on the day.
**Family and friends:** decide in advance whether you charge them full price or materials only, and record it like any other service.
**Children's styles:** price from their real timing, which is often longer than expected because of breaks.

blocks.text: Deposits and safe payments

Ask for a deposit when you buy hair for a client. A deposit of about 30% on Ifeoma's ₦13,000 style is 0.3 x 13,000 = ₦3,900; she asks for ₦4,000, which covers the ₦3,600 of hair. Write your policy in your booking confirmation: the deposit holds the slot and pays for the hair, and is carried forward once if the client gives at least a day's notice.

blocks.title: Confirm transfers in your own app
blocks.text: Fake transfer alerts and edited screenshots are a common trick. Before the client leaves, open your own bank, Opay or Moniepoint app and confirm that the money has arrived in your balance. A screenshot or an SMS is not proof of payment.

Review your prices every three months. If hair pack prices rise, or your timing log shows a style takes longer than you thought, update the menu. Tell regular clients before the change, explain it in one sentence, and keep the same quality. Clients accept fair price changes far more easily than surprise charges at the end of a service.

takeaways: A price must cover materials, consumables, your time and an overhead share.
Add a profit margin, round, and only then compare with the market.
Offer clear prices with and without hair supplied, and list add-ons separately.
Take a deposit that covers the hair you buy for a client.
Confirm every transfer in your own app before the client leaves.

activity.title: Build your price menu
steps: Choose three services you can offer now.
For each, list materials and consumables with current local prices.
Use your timing log and hourly target to price your time, and add your overhead share.
Add a profit margin, round the price, and compare with two nearby salons.
Design a one-page menu with add-ons, deposit policy and payment instructions.
activity.evidence: Your costing sheet for three services and a photo or screenshot of your finished price menu

quiz.q: Your bleach label says 5%. How much bleach do you need for 1 litre (1,000 ml) of 0.1% solution?
options: 10 ml
50 ml
100 ml
20 ml
quiz.explain: 0.1 x 1,000 ÷ 5 = 20 ml of bleach, topped up with 980 ml of water. That is 1 part bleach to 49 parts water.

quiz.q: A comb is covered in gel and hair. What is the correct order?
options: Wash with soap and water, then disinfect, rinse and dry
Soak in bleach, then wash
Wipe with a dry towel and reuse
Mix bleach with another cleaner for a stronger effect
quiz.explain: WHO guidance says clean with soap or detergent first, then disinfect. Never mix bleach with other cleaners.

quiz.q: Braiding takes 300 minutes. With a second stylist of equal speed, consultation 10, wash 30 and finishing 10 minutes stay the same. What is the total service time?
options: 350 minutes
200 minutes
175 minutes
150 minutes
quiz.explain: Braiding halves to 300 ÷ 2 = 150 minutes. 150 + 10 + 30 + 10 = 200 minutes. Only the braiding is shared.

quiz.q: Materials cost ₦4,000, time ₦6,000 and overhead share ₦500. With a 20% margin, what is the price before rounding?
A client shows a screenshot of a transfer and is about to leave. What should you do?
options: Accept the screenshot as proof
Check the SMS alert only
Ask her to forward the screenshot to your friend
Open your own bank or payment app and confirm the money is in your balance
quiz.explain: Screenshots and SMS alerts can be faked. Only your own app balance confirms the payment.

finalQuiz.q: Before agreeing to small waist-length braids, you find the client's temples are sparse and her strands are finer than sewing thread. What do you recommend?
options: Exactly what she asked, tighter at the temples
Tiny braids with extra-long hair so they last
Medium braids, shorter length, little or no added hair at the temples
A relaxer before braiding
finalQuiz.explain: Fine hair and thin edges need bigger sections, less weight and no added hair at the temples (Module 1).

finalQuiz.q: During a scalp check you find live insects and nits close to the scalp. What should you do?
options: Braid quickly before they spread
Apply a medicated shampoo you keep for this
Ask the next client to wait while you continue
Postpone, tell her privately, suggest a health worker or pharmacist, and clean your tools in hot water
finalQuiz.explain: Possible lice means postpone and refer privately. The CDC advises soaking combs in water of at least about 54°C for 5 to 10 minutes (Modules 1 and 4).

finalQuiz.q: Which consultation record best protects you if there is a dispute later?
options: A written card with style, size, length, time, price, deposit and photo consent, confirmed by her "agreed" message
A verbal agreement only
A photo of the finished style
The price written on your mirror
finalQuiz.explain: A written card plus her confirmation records exactly what was agreed (Module 1).

finalQuiz.q: Why do you wash coily hair in four to six twisted sections?
options: It uses more shampoo
It keeps the hair organised so it tangles less
It is faster to rub the whole head
So the conditioner can be skipped
finalQuiz.explain: Sectioned washing keeps coils organised and reduces tangles and breakage (Module 2).

finalQuiz.q: A client wants same-day braids and has strong medium-width hair. Which stretch fits?
options: Threading overnight
Braiding wet hair
Blow-dry on the lowest effective heat with a heat protectant
High heat to finish faster
finalQuiz.explain: Same-day braiding needs a blow-dry; the AAD advises the lowest heat setting (Module 2).

finalQuiz.q: How should you detangle a damp section?
options: Comb from roots to ends quickly
Brush it dry
Cut out every knot
Fingers first, then a wide-tooth comb from the ends upward while holding the hair above
finalQuiz.explain: Ends first, working up, with your hand taking the pull, protects the strands and the scalp (Module 2).

finalQuiz.q: A brick-lay plan has 7 rows: four rows of 9 braids and three rows of 8. Your average is 5 minutes per braid. How long is the braiding?
options: 5 hours
4 hours 40 minutes
5 hours 15 minutes
6 hours
finalQuiz.explain: 4 x 9 = 36 and 3 x 8 = 24, so 60 braids. 60 x 5 = 300 minutes, which is 5 hours, before prep and finishing (Module 3).

finalQuiz.q: You plan 50 knotless braids with 4 feed-in pieces each and get 25 pieces per pack. How many packs do you need before any spare?
finalQuiz.explain: 50 x 4 = 200 pieces. 200 ÷ 25 = 8 packs. Buy one spare if you can.

finalQuiz.q: While sealing synthetic braid ends, what is the safest practice?
options: Use a lighter on the ends near her neck
Pour boiling water over the braids on her head
Protect her neck and shoulders with a towel and dip only the ends in a cup held well below her shoulders
Seal ends before braiding with an iron
finalQuiz.explain: Hot water scalds and synthetic hair can catch fire; protect the client, keep distance and never use open flame (Module 3).

finalQuiz.q: A client returns after 10 weeks of cornrows with sore bumps at the hairline. What is the best plan?
options: Re-braid the same style tighter so it stays neat
Apply a cream from your shelf
Tell her bumps are normal
Remove the cornrows gently, rest the hairline with a low-tension style, and suggest a health worker if there is pus or it worsens
finalQuiz.explain: Bumps and soreness signal too much tension. Rest the hairline and refer when needed; never treat (Module 3).

finalQuiz.q: Your bleach is labelled 4%. How much do you need for 2 litres of 0.1% solution?
options: 50 ml
40 ml
80 ml
20 ml
finalQuiz.explain: 0.1 x 2,000 ÷ 4 = 50 ml of bleach, plus 1,950 ml of water (Module 4).

finalQuiz.q: Materials ₦5,000, time 4 hours at ₦1,500 per hour, overhead share ₦500, margin 20%. What is the price before rounding?

capstone.title: Salon service record: three clients, start to finish
capstone.brief: Deliver three complete paid or practice services to three different people and submit an evidence pack showing assessment, consultation, safe technique, tension checks, hygiene resets, timing and pricing for each.
steps: Prepare your record cards, your 0.1% disinfectant (with the dilution calculation for your bleach label), your labelled clean and used containers, and your price menu.
For each client, complete the hair assessment and scalp check, and record the serve, postpone or refer decision.
Hold a written consultation, agree style, size, length, time, price, deposit and photo consent, and get her "agreed" message.
Deliver the service: wash, detangle and stretch as needed, then install one of knotless braids, feed-in cornrows, flat twists or African threading, recording comfort scores row by row.
Time every stage in your timing log and run the full hygiene reset after each client.
Give aftercare and a takedown date in line with the AAD 2 to 3 month guidance, and send a reminder message.
Compare the actual time and cost with your quote, and adjust your menu if needed.
evidence: Three completed record cards with assessment, scalp check and consent
Before and after photos (only where consent was given) of each style
Tension logs with comfort scores for every row
Timing log for all three services with your updated averages
Your bleach dilution calculation and a photo of your labelled reset set-up
Costing sheet and final price menu with deposit and payment rules
A one-page reflection: what you would change in technique, timing and pricing
